entry.title: The power of names
entry.content:
Gregg, E. A., Bekessy, S. A., Martin, J. K., Garrard, G. E. Many IUCN red list species have names that evoke negative emotions. Human Dimensions of Wildlife. https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10871209.2020.1753132

In a nutshell: Many of the frequently used words in animal common names have high or low sentiment, and some are also associated with human emotions such as anger, fear, disgust and joy. These words may be good targets for strategic name changes to change perceptions and improve engagement with threatened species.

Animal species common names are a key communication tool between researchers, decision-makers and the public. Some of the words used in these common names are unappealing (e.g., rough-skinned horned toad), misleading (e.g., lesser bird of paradise) or even unmemorable (e.g., little grassbird). In this recent paper the authors explore the sentiment of common names and suggest that changing some of these names could be an effective, and inexpensive, way to improve engagement with and support for the conservation of threatened species.

In order to explore the sentiment and human emotions associated with certain words in common names, the authors used two sentiment lexicons to analyse the common names of 26,794 IUCN Red List animal species. First, they investigated words driving sentiment in the common names, i.e. words that are highly frequent and have particularly high- (i.e. positive) or low-scoring (i.e. negative) sentiment.

They found that the words driving sentiment varied across taxonomic status and - to a lesser extent - threat status, meaning that targets for strategic name changes will vary across these different groups. For example, 'poison' was a negative word driving sentiment in the class Amphibia, while 'lesser' was a negative word driving sentiment in Mammalia and Aves. The authors also found that some highly frequent words were associated with human emotions such as fear (e.g. 'snake') and disgust (e.g. 'rat').

This research provides insight into how small alterations in language, such as in common names, have the potential to influence perceptions. The words the authors identify (e.g. greater, golden, least, lesser, false) provide a good starting point for further research - such as controlled experimental studies - that can test more explicitly the effect of strategic name changes on perceptions and willingness to conserve species.

entry.title: Where do we want this story to go?

link.title: Where do we want this story to go?

entry.content:
My research is focused on an animal species that I never thought I would study: humans.

Specifically my research is focused on human communication. Or, even more specifically, on how we can take a more strategic approach to communications in order to encourage greater public engagement and behaviour change for biodiversity conservation.

It's a seemingly obscure topic.

But it's strangely topical right now, because the importance of clear, effective communication is rarely higher than during a global health crisis.

I recently made a post to my research lab's blog, giving some advice to conservation professionals (whoever that is...is that what I am?) about how to talk about COVID-19. In it, I discuss the important of generosity and understanding, accuracy, being clear on the purpose of communications, and being careful with use of language. These elements of communication are always important, but in a crisis situation they become critical.

I ended the piece asking myself a question:

Where do we want this story to go?

"Looking long term, it now seems undeniable that coronavirus is changing the world, and the social context in which we continue to research and work will be different even if we eventually return 'back to normal'. 

As conservation scientists we don't want to see COVID-19 create a new social and narrative context where taking action on issues like biodiversity conservation or climate change are even more difficult. As communicators, we need to think about where we want the story to go. Perhaps economic reform as a result of COVID-19 could also make progress towards a more sustainable future? Perhaps rather than bouncing back, we can bounce forward after coronavirus?"

Coronavirus is changing the world, and the new stories that emerge from these changes will set the stage for where we go next. And we all have the power to create and share these new stories.

"We can start to lay the foundation for these conversations now by avoiding comparing crises (e.g. by lamenting that biodiversity conservation hasn’t had the same response as COVID-19) and focus instead on needing kindness and cooperation, and scientific expertise. Some current responses to COVID-19 convey border control and security message frames, which don’t set a healthy narrative context for action for biodiversity conservation or climate change."

We need to avoid the stories that pull us back to where we were, and focus on the stories that push us towards where we want to be.

"By focusing instead on humanity’s ability to band together in the face of an existential crisis, and asking people to continue to have courage, we allow the space for future calls for action to tackle climate change. By highlighting that we have been able to make changes to our way of life when called for, we increase public perceptions of our collective impact and strengthen our own self-belief that we can make meaningful change.

In doing this we foster a narrative of cooperation amidst a crisis, where we listen to the advice of experts, and are able to find solutions to complex and global problems, setting the stage for progress towards a more sustainable future."

Because stories are important. They make things possible. They set the frame for our future.

Let's make it a good one.

You can find the full blog post, How to talk about COVID-19 for conservation professionals, on the ICON Science website here.

entry.title: A Selection of Pages from 2019
entry.content:
I started 2019 reading in a cabin on the beach in Simon’s Town, South Africa. I was reading outside on a deck staring out onto False Bay, a towel across my lap, sunscreen haphazardly slathered on my arms and legs, and a cap on my head. Sea air refreshing my lungs and skin from two weeks of camping in Kenya and Uganda. Thanks to the haphazard sunscreen slathering, my legs and neck were gradually turning red in strange patches throughout the day, until I retreated to the couch inside, covered in red rugs and woven cushions. Not a bad start to the year, all things considered.

In that cabin, I felt worlds away from the slums we’d passed on the drive out of Cape Town’s city centre. Simon’s Town – named after the first governor (a Dutch colonist) – felt closer to my parent’s beach house on the Victorian coastline (or the writing retreat of an aspiring upper-middle class poet), than the African savannahs I had pictured when planning my trip. This place was another continent and yet strikingly similar to home. Our trek up Table Mountain and through the Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden had been a tour of Acacia plants, whose sister’s reside in Australia. Kenya and Uganda had been filled with introduced Eucalyptus trees. I picked out two books from the cabin’s bookshelves to start my year of reading. 

First up Table Mountain: To Cape Point by Carrie Hampton. Full of beautiful pictures and information about the area. It could have been a Great Ocean Road souvenir book – a reminder of the super familiar yet different atmosphere I felt in Africa, particularly South Africa. The book didn’t feel foreign or different at all. As a white tourist, in group of white women, the strangeness of South Africa was easy to momentarily overlook. It was easy for it to look like home from different angles, from the pretty coastal landscape angles to the ugly colonial segregated (white) world-undermining angles. It was yet another colonial wake-up call. A reminder that colonisation is ongoing there and ongoing back home and I am part of it, whether I choose to see it or not and wherever on earth I am.

Next off the cabin’s shelf was Gift from the Sea by Anne Morrow Lindbergh. I can’t remember what this book was about, but it was familiar. The cut and language and smell of it reeked of childhood and books passed to me by honorary aunts and family friends. The pages were browning on the edges and the blue cover seemed imbued with sea salt. I devoured it quickly, like any human or seagull devours hot chips on the beach. GoodReads advises that it is one of those books offering musings and meanderings on life, so it makes sense I devoured it quickly in the context of a New Year and yet don’t remember any of the pieces of advice it offered.

Throughout my trip to Africa I had attempted to reread The Metamorphosis and Other Stories by Franz Kafka. It had the bonus of being a translated work that instantly put me ahead for Book Bingo for 2019 (yes, I have a Book Bingo for the year, shush you). I had read The Metamorphosis before, but Kafka’s shorter stories offered fragments of social commentary that felt meaningful and timely to start a year of personal and political change. Still, not that easy to read. I finished it back home rotating between my bed, my garden lined with jasmine flowers and the lounge room lined with a million cushions.

From there I also read The Old Man and the Sea by Ernest Hemingway. A classic that’s been sitting on my bookshelf for a while and I had never read. It seems it’s my curse to be forever disappointed by the classics. I enjoy the language and the insight to everyday life they offer, but otherwise my 21st century plot-focused mind is forever waiting for the twist or conflict or world-shattering reveal in the final moments. Perhaps Game of Thrones has forever ruined slice of life content for me, or I should pre-read synopses to know what I’m in for before I hang out for twists when the book is simply about an old man and the sea (and musings on life and death and meaning etc.).

At Clunes Book Festival 2019 (one of my favourite places and events in the entire world) I purchased upwards of 17 books, including two copies of Aviary Wonders Inc. Spring Catalog and Instruction Manual by Kate Samworth. A satirical, beautiful, heart-wrenching, existential piece of art that you definitely shouldn’t gift to anyone, because anyone who would appreciate this book will find it completely depressing and everyone else just won’t get it. But you should. Get it, I mean. The book imagines a scenario where all birds are extinct and offers a catalogue for designing your own perfect bird. Out of all the books I’ve read this book summarises 2019 best for me, which is rather depressing. The past few years has seen the state of the climate discussed somewhat more productively in the media. The School Strikes have done much to mainstream calls for action, there is a gradual shift from a focus on individual behaviours to systemic changes needed, and the Australian Conservation Foundation (alongside other media, non-for-profit and political groups) weren’t wrong when they labelled the Australian Federal Election the 'climate election'. Yet the outcome of that election was rotten for the environment, the current Australian government is currently working on tearing down so-called “green tape” (which, to be frank, is already as weak as ‘tape’ sounds), and it looks like hardly any country is going to meet their climate targets.

In times like this, it sometimes feels immensely privileged of me to be focused on issues of biodiversity conservation and extinction rather than climate change or other social issues. Yet these issues are inherently linked, and our biggest problems involve both of them. The drying up of the Murray Darling is bad for water and bad for fish biodiversity. We lose species (i.e. biodiversity), we lose important functions of ecosystems, ecosystems that we have already altered beyond recognition. We still don’t quite understand the repercussions of all this, but I’ll let you in on a little secret: it ain’t good. I don’t think it’s useful to discuss my existential/apocalyptic fears too much here, but I think it’s important to consider (especially given recent events) that the changing climate is already impacting people around the world. Even if those people aren’t us or our loved ones yet, I reckon we should start to do something to create a better future for all of us.

But let’s push aside those dark thoughts for today and turn to nicer things, like book recommendations from friends! This year I was recommended The Lagoon: How Aristotle Invented Science by Armand Marie Leroi. This book took me way too long to read. My excuse is that while it was beautifully written, it was dense and difficult for me to read after a day PhD-ing. Recommend to science writing and philosophy of science nerds. It is truly beautiful and fascinating, but requires some energy. I was also recommended The Village Effect: Why Face-to-Face Contact is Good for Our Health, Happiness, Learning, and Longevity by Susan Pinker. This book feels like a long-form The Guardian or The Conversation science article, and I don’t know whether that’s a good or bad thing. I think it’s a good thing because it’s easy to read and packed full of interesting information. I think it’s a bad thing because I feel like I quickly scrolled/scanned through and only learnt what I already knew and/or believed to be true. Basically having friends and a partner is good unless you get fooled by an identity thief. But yeah, self-care / socialising is important for everyone, we’re social animals go figure. (In hindsight, I appreciate that the friend/s recommending this to me were probably trying to subtly tackle my PhD stress.)

After years of slowly chipping away on holidays, in courtyards and in the aforementioned cushion-infested lounge room I finally finished Alan Turing: The Enigma by Andrew Hodges. I honestly think this book is written very well considering its content and dutiful focus on the mathematical research of Alan Turing. However, it was incredibly difficult for me to read after a day at the office, and, honestly, maybe I just don’t care enough about maths (gasp!). Alan Turing’s story is fascinating, horrible and important, but the interesting parts weren’t enough for me to muster up the focus needed to comprehend the detail of his work. My favourite parts were when the author discussed in simpler language the importance of Turing’s work, as well as the final chapters when he discussed in detail the social context and attitudes around homosexuality in his final years as well as the years preceding. Highly recommend to maths/computer/engineering-focused friends. But otherwise, just read some Wikipedia pages and save yourself a year or two.

Thanks to my own reluctance to give up on some of the more challenging reads discussed above (as well as my own distraction by other important facets of life…), I didn’t meet my reading goal for this year. I definitely didn’t read enough to write a post with my favourite books of the year, let alone my favourite science or natural history writing. But so be it. I’m ending the year in my adorably shaky share house, reading some delightfully distracting fiction, being talked into playing video games by my housemates, and getting excited for a busy, challenging, climate-tackling 2020. Come at me.

entry.title: A waterless barrier could halt cane toad spread in Western Australia

link.title: A waterless barrier could halt cane toad spread in Western Australia

entry.content:
A chance to briefly return to my ecological roots occurred recently with the publication of my Masters paper in Conservation Science and Practice.

https://twitter.com/SciEms/status/1141203264429383680?s=20

This paper tests the on-ground feasibility of a waterless barrier to halt cane toad spread in Western Australia.

The waterless barrier strategy capitalises on the cane toad's reliance on artificial water points, specifically within a thin corridor of toad-friendly habitat between Broome and Port Hedland, squeezed between the ocean and the Great Sandy Desert.

[caption id="" align="aligncenter" width="417"] Figure 1. Map of the study area. Toads were collected around Kununurra, and transported to Wallal Downs Station in the Kimberley–Pilbara corridor. The invasion front was just southwest of Halls Creek during the time of the study (invasion front, as of 2017, shown as solid black line). Predicted cane toad distribution (based on breeding season length) is shown in grey shades.[/caption]

During the wet season, toads are expected to move through the corridor landscape without issue. However, during the dry season we expect toads will be reliant on artificial water bodies, such as pastoral dams.

Making these water bodies inaccessible to toads (e.g. by raising troughs and sealing leaks) will make this area inhospitable for toads and therefore prevent their movement across the corridor and into the ecologically and culturally rich Pilbara region. The corridor need only be wide enough (~70km) to account for toad movement during the wet season.

My project was specifically based around testing concerns from stakeholders around assumptions previous simulation modelling had made about the corridor landscape. For example, how could we be sure that cane toads wouldn't survive the dry season through other means? What about deep goanna burrows, protective coastal vegetation or coastal fogs?

I aimed to directly test these concerns on the ground by translocating and radio-tracking cane toads within the barrier corridor. I did this using male cane toads only to eliminate the possibility of establishing a population ahead of the toad invasion front.

[caption id="attachment_96" align="aligncenter" width="561"] A cane toad with the radio transmitter on. Image: R. Hayes[/caption]

I then tested the survival, movement rates, and use of shelter sites of toads across two kinds of habitat within the corridor (coastal and desert).

The toads were incredibly adept at finding shelter sites and moved some impressive distances. One particularly speedy toad moved 2.54km in one night! One of the largest single-night movements ever recorded in an anuran!

However, the toads only survived 2-3 days in this landscape, and the maximum predicted survival time was 5 days. In addition, contrary to what we expected, survival was higher in the desert habitat as compared to the coastal habitat.

entry.title: Chasing Mr Toad
entry.content:
If there was a time in my life when I was absolutely dripping in sweat, then this was it.

There were beads of the stuff all over my face, and I was leaning into a blast of musty air con, only moving away to gulp down some electrolytes. I suppose that may sound like hell, but honestly, I was having the time of my life.

Welcome to fieldwork.

I was taking shelter in a dusty 4WD on a cattle station, sitting on the coast between Broome and Port Hedland in Western Australia. More importantly, I was chasing down a rather infamous Australian pest: the Cane Toad (Rhinella marina).

[caption id="attachment_82" align="alignnone" width="3888"] ...and here we have Mr Toad wearing a stunning ball chain belt complete with radio transmitter. Photo: R Hayes[/caption]

While us ecologists are usually keen on keeping our study species around, I was wishing this particular Mr Toad would go back to South America, and leave our poor native predators alone. Unfortunately, that ship sailed in 1935, and over the past 80 years the toad has thrived in our landscape.

With no natural predators, the toad is free to breed more efficiently than rabbits, and spread wherever the climate permits it. Any native animal attempting to take a bite of a toad at best end up reviling at the taste, and at worst are taken out by the toad’s toxin, resulting in species declines. The toad is now established in the north of Western Australia, and is expected to continue moving south-west towards the Pilbara, in the south of Western Australia.

This is what brought me to a cattle station in the middle of Western Australia.

The station sits within the so-called Kimberley-Pilbara corridor, an area which should be inhospitable to toads during the dry season, when all the natural water dries up. But this is cattle country, and so there are man-made water sources everywhere. And many of them leak.

[caption id="attachment_85" align="alignnone" width="3888"] Leaking pastoral tanks can result in massive pools of cane toad happy-places. Photo: R Hayes[/caption]

Previous computer simulations had predicted that by effectively removing these water sources (by upgrading infrastructure and preventing leaks), a barrier would be created, preventing toads from moving southwards towards the Pilbara.

But this idea needed on-ground testing. Enter me: a bright-eyed master’s student, keen for a challenging field project.

After half a year of writing and reviewing grant applications, ethics proposals and Park’s permits, I flew to Kununurra in Western Australia to collect 20 male toads and drive them down south to a cattle station within the barrier area.

Yes, I was moving a non-native animal into new territory; a horrible idea in most ecological circles. But these toads were all males (to prevent any breeding), and we were releasing them in a remote area far away from available water sources. More importantly, the toads were going to be radio-tracked intensively as part of my study, so the risk of establishment was ultimately minimal.

The waterless barrier strategy assumes that toads will be able to survive within the corridor during the wet season with no issues. During the dry, however, artificial water points (i.e. dams and tanks) should be the only water available to toads, meaning their removal will prevent their survival and create a barrier. The barrier simply needs to be wide enough to account for toad dispersal through the unrestrictive wet season.

But there were a few untested assumptions around previous work. Were we sure toads couldn’t survive here without those artificial water sources? What about shelter sites, such as goanna burrows? What about coastal fogs providing moisture through morning dew?

To answer these questions, I started by attaching a radio transmitter to each toad by measuring out little belts made from a ball chain and clipping them around the toads’ waists. They were released at night into the desert, far away from any artificial water sources.

[caption id="attachment_87" align="alignnone" width="3888"] A gorgeous landscape to be working in. Absolutely filled with ankle-twisting and toad-sheltering goanna burrows. Photo: R Hayes[/caption]

The following morning myself and a research volunteer rose early and went out to catch up with the toads. Waving an antenna around like madmen, we listened desperately for the tell-tale BEEP leading us to a sheltering toad.

One of the ways toads have adapted to the Australian landscape is through being active at night and sheltering during the day. In doing this they avoid the worst of the heat, reduce their water loss, and increase their survival ability.

We were therefore expecting the toads to shelter during the day, allowing us to determine which shelter sites they were selecting within the landscape. For the most part, they did (60% of the time, in fact), however, we found one headstrong individual not only not sheltering, but hopping along during the heat of the day!

Indeed, even sheltering toads moved substantial distances overnight, far above the distances we expected. One avid sprinter managed to move over 2.5 km in one night!

It's unsurprising then that occasionally a BEEP could not be found, and we had no choice but to trudge through the desert in 500 m blocks, heading up to 3 km away from our starting point, all in search of one singular spirited cane toad and the valuable data he represented. Never have I desired a dune buggy more.

Even once we tracked the BEEP to its source, finding the toads was not always easy. The toads were brilliant at finding shelter sites within the landscape, and within this landscape the majority of shelter sites were goanna burrows.

This meant that we often had to stick an inspection camera down the burrows to confirm exactly where the toads were. This also helped us to avoid sticking our hands down into potential snake territory...

 

[caption id="attachment_336" align="alignnone" width="2128"] Goanna burrows at two different study sites: the desert and coastal habitats. One of these is better shelter than the other...[/caption]

Once we finally found our toad, I weighed them to approximate their water loss, and recorded their GPS coordinates and shelter site type, such as a goanna burrow or shrub.

As part of our ethics requirements, we planned to humanely euthanise toads once they had lost 40% of their body weight (toads can survive losing 50%). Unfortunately, due to their unexpected speediness (and the harshness of the corridor environment), we were unable to locate many toads before they reached critical dehydration.

While an undoubtedly grim experience for the toads (and an emotional and philosophical trial for their human followers), this short survival time is ultimately a positive outcome for the waterless barrier strategy.

[caption id="" align="aligncenter" width="2128"] Plots showing survival (i.e., proportion of individuals alive) over time. (a) Overall survival. Dashed lines indicate 95% confidence intervals. (b) Effect of habitat on survival. * indicates censored points where a lost toad was last seen alive[/caption]

Most toads only survived 1-2 days, and our analysis predicts a maximum survival time of 5 days in this environment, supporting the assumption that toads cannot survive in this area without access to artificial water sources.

In the end, this project indicates that the waterless barrier is a feasible means to halt cane toad movement down the west Australian coast. This relatively inexpensive strategy could therefore be an effective way to protect species in the Pilbara from the toad's impact.

For my part, this project was my first taste of real field work and my first experience within Australia's vast semi-arid and arid environments, which I've since fallen in love with. If you're someone who has never left the eastern coast I absolutely insist you go out and explore more of this exceptional country.

I myself can't wait to get back out there.

Simple study question: Can cane toads survive in a potential barrier area without access to artificial water bodies during the dry season?

Simple study answer: No. The model predicts a maximum survival of 5 days in this environment. (Gregg et al. 2019).

Importance: Supports the waterless barrier strategy, allaying fears that toads would be able to survive in the barrier despite the removal of artificial water bodies.

In a word: Barrier

entry.title: Messaging (and strategy) matters: a new systematic review

link.title: Messaging (and strategy) matters: a new systematic review

entry.content:
I’m happy to share a new paper, again led by my lab mate Lindall Kidd (who remains steadfast in her disinterest in setting up a social media profile, much to my admiration and awe).

Messaging Matters. Our new systematic review of conservation messaging Kidd et al. (great people to work with!). 50 days free access in Biological Conservation https://t.co/LdpkCIiW7Y pic.twitter.com/R5ciqlSYR2

— Matthew Selinske (@M_Selinske) May 27, 2019

https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js

In this review, we aimed to explore the state of conservation messaging research, including the extent to which studies are drawing from other disciplines.

We considered papers through the lens of strategic communication. Strategic communication is an umbrella term that can be used to describe any kind of purposeful communication, and draws from fields such as advertising, public relations, and mass communications.

For this reason, strategic communication can be a useful lens for interdisciplinary work, as it allows for flexibility when considering the benefits of different theoretical approaches (e.g. marketing, behaviour change etc.).

[caption id="attachment_78" align="alignnone" width="1778"] Figure 1: A schematic representation of strategic communication design steps using theory as a conceptual framework. Campaign design steps are shown above the arrow, and the relevant application of theory with examples at each stage is described below. Adapted from Noar (2006).[/caption]

To investigate conservation messaging research, we systematically reviewed the literature, using Web of Science, by searching for articles using the search terms: (“framing” OR “marketing” OR “messaging”) AND (“conservation” OR “environment”) AND “biodiversity” OR “species”).

We excluded papers that did not include at least one of the following research purposes: 1) to document a case study that describes an existing message; 2) to develop theory relating to conservation messaging; or 3) to conduct an experiment to test a theory or contribute to the design aspect of a message. After this, we were left with 89 papers for analysis.

Results show that conservation messaging is an emerging research area, with the oldest study published in 1995, and 69% of studies being published in the last five years.

The most common messaging aims in the papers were to increase awareness, educate people, and/or encourage behaviour change (see Figure 2). While eliminating knowledge gaps can be a useful first step, a 'knowledge-deficit' approach can be limited in encouraging behaviour change. Therefore researchers would perhaps benefit from focusing more on messaging aims that go beyond increasing awareness.

[caption id="attachment_85" align="aligncenter" width="491"] Figure 2. The aim of messaging studies in the peer reviewed academic literature, based on a systematic search of Web of Science. Other aims of reviewed papers included assessment of the terms used in policy discourse.[/caption]

Framing and marketing were the most commonly used theoretical approaches. Overall, the theories used spanned disciplines such as psychology, marketing and communication, however, some studies did not appear to be grounded in established theories relevant to their research aim. For example, almost one third of reviewed studies stated that their research aim was to encourage behavioural change, yet few studies used behaviour change theories such as the Theory of Planned Behaviour (Ajzen 1991). Fourteen papers did not indicate that their research was guided by theory.

Similarly, while citations in the reviewed papers spanned many disciplines, the majority were within the environmental sciences and biodiversity conservation (see Figure 3). Therefore, the opportunity remains to draw more thoroughly from other disciplines, particularly when taking an explicit theoretical or disciplinary approach, such as psychology or marketing.

[caption id="attachment_83" align="alignnone" width="1337"] Figure 3. The top ten Web of Science research disciplines of 4811 papers cited within a set of reviewed conservation messaging papers (n= 89).[/caption]

One third of reviewed studies did not state a target audience for their message. Of the fifty-eight that did, 27 targeted a mass audience and 33 targeted a defined audience segment.

In addition, only one third of studies targeted a segmented audience, despite many employing a marketing approach. Audience segmentation is a key element of any marketing campaign and is crucial for effective strategic targeting and message design. Therefore, a major research gap highlighted by this review is the lack of audience segmentation. 

A lack of audience targeting also makes it difficult to evaluate the effectiveness of a messaging campaign. Adopting a strategic approach from the outset – through clear grounding in theory, and specific identification of aims and audiences – should assist in ensuring evaluation of a messaging strategy can occur effectively. 

The review showed that all experimental studies evaluated the effectiveness of message design using pre- and post-measures of a dependent variable, and a control group. Most relied on self-reported measures (e.g., behavioural intention). Only five studies evaluated specific behavioural change. Over one third of case studies undertook no evaluation.

Recommendations:

  • Consider messaging aims that go beyond increasing awareness (e.g., consider other mechanisms that motivate behaviour change, such as social norms or self-efficacy)
  • Ground studies in established theories and approaches relevant to the research aim
  • Draw from literature in disciplines relevant to the research aim and approach
  • Target relevant audiences using audience segmentation techniques
  • Adopt a strategic approach from the outset to allow for effective evaluation

Kidd, LR., Garrard, GE., Bekessy, SA., Mills, M., Camilleri, A., Fidler, F., Fielding, K., Gordon, A., Gregg, EA., Kusmanoff, A., Louis, W., Moon, K., Robinson, JA., Selinske, M., Shanahan, D., Adams, V. (2019) Messaging matters: a systematic review of the conservation messaging literature. Biological Conservation. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biocon.2019.05.020

entry.title: When in doubt, go to the library

link.title: When in doubt, go to the library

entry.content:
Need some holiday reading? Gift ideas? Just want an excuse to buy some vaguely work-related novels and knock off early?

I've got you covered.

I've managed to read a few stellar books this year, many of which focus around the environment or natural history in one way or another, and all of which I highly recommend (to the right audience of course). So read on for my bookish recommendations in no particular order!

1. The Tapir's Morning Bath: Mysteries of the tropical rain forest and the scientists who are trying to solve them, Elizabeth Royte

For conservation scientists, ecologists, researchers (particularly students), and anyone wanting an inside look into their world

Okay, I'm cheating right off the bat because I did not read this book this year (although I've been known to leaf through and reread sections on bad days). However, I think it's worth a mention because this book is one of my absolute favourites and a major inspiration for this blog.

It centres around Barro Colorado Island in the middle of the Panama Canal, where our journalist writer follows around a force of scientists who are each trying to understand their own little part of the isolated rain forest. From monkey dung to philosophical meanderings on the goals of conservation science itself, this book has it all. The (real-life) characters are a joy to meet, and their academic / career struggles and fears will no doubt feel familiar to any student or wannabe academic.

2. Defending Biodiversity: Environmental Science and Ethics, Jonathan A. Newman

For academics, philosophers, debaters, and anyone interested in environmental issues

This was the first book I read in 2018, and while it felt like reading a textbook at times (welcome to academic texts), it was overall very illuminating. The book outlines and assesses major arguments for conserving biodiversity, considering both the instrumental (e.g. ecosystem services) or intrinsic (e.g. natural beauty) value of nature.

I would expect only the most dedicated to read this from top to tail – I myself was mainly  motivated by the need to write this book review – but I would genuinely recommend it for anyone interested in rethinking or interrogating their own ethics and arguments around biodiversity conservation, or indeed environmental issues in general. It's sure to add an edge to your future arguments.

3. Hidden Museum: A Cabinet of Curiosities, Shaun Parr

For curiosity seekers and short attention spans

This book here is at the entire other end of the spectrum when it comes to length and density. A borderline coffee table book, with very little text, this one is aptly named. It is simply a small collection of curiosities, focused around natural history. It also comes with a little red 'magnifying glass' so you can explore the pages yourself. I’ll say no more.

4. Hidden Nature: A Voyage of Discovery, Alys Fowler

For those in need of a holiday

I bought this book because of its beautiful cover and because I needed a break. This book provided exactly that. A perfect, breezy holiday read. You basically get to spend the entire book exploring Birmingham's canal network via kayak and watching the writer's garden grow (alongside an emotional internal journey).

This is a well-written book, but not a page-turner and certainly not action packed. In other words, give it to your "gardening gran" friend, not your "let's watch Mad Max: Fury Road again" friend.

5. The Sound of a Wild Snail Eating, Elisabeth Tova Bailey

For people who enjoy watching ants in the garden

Like Hidden Nature this one is a delightful, peaceful, and beautifully written book. However rather than a broad focus on canal environments, this little book focuses on a little subject: snails.

The bed-ridden narrator focuses our chaotic minds on the life of one small snail. She manages to drift in and out of snail physiology and evolution without breaking the captivating tone of the book. Great for a weekend read in your garden, or a mental health day in bed.

6. Dark Emu, Bruce Pascoe

For Australians

Recommended to me by many, I finally managed to cross this book off my “to-read” list. An absolutely fascinating (and worldview-shaking) look at the lives of precolonial Aboriginal Australians, particularly focused on their land use and management.

This book is jam-packed with evidence sourced primarily from early Australian colonial explorers, alongside frank and open language making it a particularly compelling and engaging read. Highly recommend to all.

Happy reading!

entry.title: Seeds in the Sand
entry.content:
I may be a little biased, but I find the Australian semi-arid landscape simply stunning.

What appears to be a desolate place on the surface suddenly bursts to life once you simply kneel down to the ground and take a proper look.

Down there you can see tracks left by bettongs hurtling through the sand the night before. You can see bustling rodent highways, trails left by an innumerable number of tiny rodent feet, lining the dunes. You can see seedlings sprouting from piles of sand excavated by bilbies. And after rain, you can see ancient shield shrimp scuttling around shallow, muddy puddles.

[caption id="attachment_307" align="aligncenter" width="3996"] A smattering of tracks at the Arid Recovery reserve, including one of my favourites: the Shingleback / Sleepy / Stumpy-tail Lizard's tracks.[/caption]

But while the arid landscape is littered with signs of diverse animal life, the plant life is similarly spectacular. The red sand and gibber plains which overwhelm the horizon are contrasted by plains of saltbush, shiny leaves of hopbush, and the grey-blue stillness of mulga trees.  And after a burst of rain the sudden addition of bright green vegetation is striking against the red sand.

So while many zoologists (we’re all friends here) sigh audibly at the mere mention of vegetation surveys, they simply don’t feel tiresome out here. And in any case, there’s something rather relaxing and peaceful about vegetation surveys.

They’re methodical and relatively quiet. There’s no animal handling stress (from either party, to our knowledge), no quick processing of a reluctant strong-kicking marsupial, and no peanut-allergy-inducing baits to put my confused immune system on red alert.

Perhaps most exciting is that vegetation surveys allow us to explore species which are so incredibly different from ourselves, species which can tower over us and spread their roots beneath our feet. Just take a moment, zoologists, and admit it (even if just to yourself): plants are pretty damn cool.

[caption id="attachment_308" align="aligncenter" width="3996"] The striking arid vegetation, and some evidence of herbivory...[/caption]

So there I was, out in the field again, wedging two pieces of a deconstructed ice-cream container into the ground and taking a sizeable sample of sand using a spoon as a shovel. Ecologists are nothing if not resourceful.

I imagine me carting giant snap-lock bags filled with sand across each dune made it appear as though I desperately wanted to take the entire desert home with me. But I was actually collecting a seed bank for PhD candidate, Charlotte Mills, who at that point was walking around with a giant square made out of piping, sampling plant species within quadrats (hence the giant square made out of piping).

Charlotte had set up exclusion pens throughout the Arid Recovery reserve, in order to investigate the pressure that the reintroduced herbivores were putting on the plants. By comparing between exclusion pens, which controlled which animals were allowed in, Charlotte was able to determine to what extent certain animals, such as the reintroduced Burrowing Bettong, Plains Mouse, and Hopping Mouse, were having an effect on the vegetation.

[caption id="attachment_315" align="aligncenter" width="3264"] The exclusion pens from above... Images: Charlotte Mills[/caption]

By having many sites set up on many dunes inside the Arid Recovery reserve, Charlotte ensured her results would be applicable across a broad landscape. She also carried out similar work in the Strzelecki desert, to consider how different communities of animals can drive differences in the vegetation. Within the Arid Recovery reserve Charlotte had 10 sites to monitor.

On the ground, this meant we had a lot of work to do. For each site we had to:

  1. Walk transects for tracks and scats to determine the animal community within each fenced site i.e. which animals and how many?
  2. Randomly sample the plant community through quadrat sampling (enter giant square made out of piping)
  3. Check up on the growth and health state of larger shrubs and trees

Those were the basics that Charlotte was monitoring every field trip as the centre of her research. Basics that would hopefully answer the question: what impact do herbivores (plant-eaters) and granivores (seed-eaters) have on vegetation communities?

But as researchers, we’re curious. And no matter how focused we are on a central question, others always crop up. This happens fairly often out in the field, where there’s always some element we haven’t considered. The trick is to notice the relevant ones.

Charlotte had noticed two.

What if the animals were ruining the chance of plants growing from the very beginning? What if they were eating the seeds hiding beneath the sand, seeds still waiting to germinate?

Cut to me on my knees, sampling dirt (or rather, a seed bank!) with a spoon. By looking closely at the seed bank, Charlotte could see if the bettongs and mice were changing which plants might have the opportunity to grow, and whether any were being eaten out of house and home!

Charlotte had also noticed that there was so much soil turnover at some of the incredibly active sites, which were absolutely littered with a mess of bettong tracks, that she tended to see less spider holes around. Out in this desert environment, spiders live in neat, impressive little holes and they’re a fairly common sight among the dunes. Could the mass of bettongs be messing with the spider’s ability to maintain reliable hidey holes?

We needed some data on this. So Charlotte decided to start counting spider holes as part of the tracks and scats transect.

[caption id="attachment_310" align="aligncenter" width="3996"] Fun Fact! Spider holes are incredibly hard for a non-expert with an iPhone camera to capture in focus...[/caption]

I happily completed the spider hole counting for a time. There are so many different kinds of spider (or ‘spidey’ for the professional ecologist) holes and they’re all damn fascinating. Some are made by the famous trapdoor spiders, but even those kinds vary from neat little flaps to giant openings disguised with leaf litter and grass.

Some are edged with vegetation that appears woven together forming gorgeous patterns around the dig. Others are so small that I could only determine it was a spider hole by peering in and spotting a scrunched up bunch of minute, hairy legs. All of these digs were so incredibly perfect: perfectly circular, perfectly smooth inside. They looked human-made, mechanically made. Spiders are truly incredible engineers.

There were a few moments, however, when my fascination was overshadowed by a primal fear of our eight-legged friends. Once in particular, I gazed around the exclusion pen, scanning the immense number of spider burrows around me, one after the other. I glanced down at the inordinately large tally on my notepad, and realised I was in a city of spiders. Well and truly surrounded.

While I set about dreamily peering into tiny burrows and musing over spider populations, Charlotte was set on truly investigating this question from as many angles as possible.

[caption id="attachment_312" align="aligncenter" width="3264"] Drone photos of the red sand. You can even spot animal tracks from this height! Images: Charlotte Mills[/caption]

Before we started trampling across each site – and carting away mounds of soil – Charlotte mustered the latest in human technology and took aerial photographs using a drone. These photographs allowed Charlotte to step away from the precise details we were collecting and visualise at a broad level the differences between her different fence treatments.

(Charlotte tells me she has since adorned her supervisor’s external office walls with drone pictures of red sand, shrubs and fences).

The Australian landscape has borne witness to some dramatic changes in its time. Since western colonisation invasive rabbits have had a dramatic effect on vegetation, and many of our native mammals have been pushed out, leaving us with little understanding of what makes a healthy, functioning ecosystem.

As a result, we can’t always be sure what is needed to properly ‘rewild’ damaged areas. Charlotte’s field work alone has already highlighted gaps in our knowledge, and drawn attention to complexities within the ecological communities we’re trying to recreate.

Charlotte’s results on this project are forthcoming, but to satiate your hunger for seeds, reintroduced mammals and what these mean for our landscapes, you can see some of Charlotte’s published work here and here.

Simple study question: What impact do herbivores have on vegetation communities?

Simple study answer: Different animals eat different things and in varying amounts!

Importance: Vital for understanding how our ecological communities work and how we can effectively ‘rewild’ modified landscapes.

In a word: Communities.

Read more about Charlotte’s research on her website here.
